To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the tree allocation rule outperforms the linear discriminant and the logistic regression procedures in the majority of the cases, (2) the tree rule is robust to assumption violations, and (3) the tree rule performs well when the group-conditional densities are multimodal and the linear discriminant procedure performs poorly

(i) the tree rule has good performance relative to the linear discriminant and logit procedures and is not very sensitive to violations of the assumptions of the linear discriminant rule and (ii) the tree rule is more robust to the violation of the assumptions of linear discriminant rule than the logit procedure

(a) the tree rule has a lower misclassification error rate than the linear discriminant and the logistic regression rules, and (b) the tree rule can be used regardless (i.e., without assuming any knowledge about) the underlying group-conditional distributions, whereas the linear discriminant rule cannot be used when the group-conditional variances are not equal, and the logistic regression rule cannot be used if the group-conditional distribution is not binomial.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of classification procedures that do not require knowledge of the underlying group-conditional distributions.
the development of classification procedures that can handle data that are not normally distributed.
the development of classification rules which do not rely on the assumption that the group-conditional densities are known or that they are members of some parametric family.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the tree rule performs as well as the other methods and is a viable alternative when there is no a priori information on which to base the classification procedure.
tree-structured allocation is a useful classification procedure, especially in situations where assumptions of other parametric classification procedures cannot be made.
the authors' tree rule performs as well as the other procedures and in certain cases better.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the tree rule is a robust classification procedure that can be used in a wide range of applications.
tree-structured allocation procedures provide a viable alternative to parametric classification methods.
the tree rule is a robust and efficient alternative for classifying observations into populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the tree rule can be used in situations where the linear discriminant and/or logistic regression rules fail.
, for many data sets, the tree rule performs at least as well as the other procedures.

the tree rule is a viable classification procedure that does not rely on any assumptions regarding the group-conditional density functions and is robust to certain violations of the assumption of equal covariance matrices.
